title: Yash Patil, 23, Sells AI Startup Applied Compute to Palo Alto for $4.5 Billion
excerpt: The Indian American co-founder, who left Stanford for OpenAI at 20, built Applied Compute from an idea in January 2025 to a $100 million revenue run-rate — and will become Palo Alto Networks' Co-Chief AI Officer when the all-stock deal closes.
body:
• Palo Alto Networks announced on November 18 that it will acquire Applied Compute, the AI startup co-founded by 23-year-old Indian American Yash Patil, in an all-stock transaction valued at $4.5 billion, subject to adjustments.
  • Applied Compute was founded in 2025 by Patil with fellow Stanford alumni and former OpenAI researchers Rhythm Garg and Linden Li; Patil will become Palo Alto Networks' Co-Chief AI Officer when the deal closes.
  • The startup grew from zero revenue to more than $100 million in annualized revenue run-rate in just over 18 months, and was valued at $3.25 billion in a funding round weeks before the acquisition was announced.
  • The deal is not closed: it needs regulatory clearance and is expected to complete in Palo Alto Networks' fiscal third quarter of 2027, which ends April 30, 2027.

Palo Alto Networks has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Applied Compute, a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models, in an all-stock transaction valued at $4.5 billion, the company announced on November 18. The startup behind the deal is barely 18 months old, and its co-founder and chief executive, Yash Patil, is 23.

What Applied Compute does

Applied Compute helps companies adapt open-weight AI models using their own information and run them in environments they choose. Palo Alto Networks said the acquisition will bring Applied Compute's platform and AI research team in-house to help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both — including in sovereign cloud environments built to meet local compliance rules. Applied Compute will continue to serve AI-native companies, digital natives and large enterprises, and Palo Alto Networks will bring the platform to its global customer base. Its enterprise client roster has been reported to include Microsoft, Shopify, DoorDash, Harvey, Cognition, Clay and Decagon.

"We built Applied Compute with an exceptional team of AI researchers and engineers to make it easy for any company to train, serve, and improve proprietary models."

— Yash Patil, Co-Founder and CEO, Applied Compute

Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, said the company had evaluated Applied Compute firsthand as a prospective customer. "Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured," Arora said. "Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we've seen, and its research team is exceptional."

From Austin and Stanford to OpenAI

Patil was born to Indian immigrant parents and grew up in Austin, Texas, where he attended the Liberal Arts and Science Academy; his father worked on circuit design and power architecture at Qualcomm and Arm. At Stanford University, where he studied computer science, he met OpenAI chief Sam Altman at a dinner Altman hosted, then emailed him about the chatbot team. He joined OpenAI's residency program at 20 and worked on post-training infrastructure and on what became Codex, the company's coding tool. He left Stanford to start Applied Compute in 2025 with Rhythm Garg, 24, and Linden Li, 25 — both fellow Stanford students and OpenAI researchers.

An 18-month run

The idea behind Applied Compute began taking shape in January 2025. By April 2026, the company had reached unicorn status after securing $80 million in funding from Kleiner Perkins at a valuation of $1.3 billion, according to The American Bazaar. Earlier this month it raised $350 million at a $3.25 billion valuation. With a team of just a few dozen people, it grew from zero revenue to more than $100 million in annualized revenue run-rate in just over 18 months. The $4.5 billion acquisition price is about 38 percent above that most recent valuation, though the final value is subject to adjustments and the number of shares has not been fixed. The founders have not disclosed their stakes, so Patil's personal payout from the deal is unconfirmed.

What happens next

The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory clearance and US antitrust review, and is expected to close in Palo Alto Networks' fiscal third quarter of 2027, which runs from February through April 2027. When it closes, the Applied Compute team will join Palo Alto Networks and Patil will become its Co-Chief AI Officer. Palo Alto Networks said it expects the acquisition to add over $1 billion to its Next-Generation Security annual recurring revenue by fiscal 2029. For now, both companies continue to operate independently, and the platform Patil's team built keeps serving its existing customers.
